paragraphs.text: The invention of air conditioning provides a useful introduction to the mysterious question of where good ideas come from. It sums up how we generally think about inventions. One night in 1902, a young American engineer, Willis Carrier, was waiting for a train, watching the fog roll across the platform, when he had a sudden flash of insight: he could exploit the principle of fog to cool buildings. He patented the idea, put his invention into production, and made a fortune. Over a hundred years later, the still-surviving Carrier Corporation was generating annual sales worth $15 billion. But what’s really interesting about this narrative is how unusual it is: big new ideas are almost never born like that. It’s very rare to find a case where somebody working alone, in a moment of sudden clarity, has a great breakthrough that changes the world.

However, a surprising truth about big ideas is that the people who come up with them often subsequently claim that the inspiration came instantly. Charles Darwin, the British scientist usually credited with the theory of evolution, always said that the theory occurred to him on 28 September 1838 while he was reading Thomas Malthus’s essay on population: suddenly the mechanism of evolution seemed blindingly straightforward. Yet Darwin’s own notebooks reveal that the theory was forming in his mind more than a year beforehand. Darwin may well have simply convinced himself of the flash of inspiration.

Chance works in many ways. One is the unintended event. One day in 1839, Charles Goodyear, a hardware salesman, was carrying out experiments as he had been doing for quite some time, trying to make a useful material out of rubber. But he found the rubber broke when cold, and melted in high heat. Goodyear then tried mixing it with sulphur, and accidentally dropped the mixture onto a hot stove. He suddenly realised that the rubber had become more solid, yet flexible. Goodyear had vulcanised rubber, a process that gives it useful properties and makes it possible to use today in everything from golf balls to car tyres. Unfortunately for Goodyear, his discovery never brought him the fortune he deserved. When he died in 1860, he was more than $200,000 in debt.

Of course, what is most important about an unintended event is the creative way it is used. Take Percy Spencer. One day in 1945, Spencer was walking through his lab at the Raytheon Company, when he stopped briefly by a magnetron – the tube that produces high-frequency microwaves to power radar for things like missile-defence systems. He had a chocolate bar in his pocket and suddenly realised it had melted. Immediately, Spencer imagined what this could be used for and the result was eventually the creation of the microwave oven. Someone else might well have just cursed the mess in their pocket.

One useful way of looking at invention is the notion of the ‘adjacent possible’ which describes a process that initially seems like common sense, but is actually an entirely new way of looking at almost everything. The term, first used by biologist Stuart Kauffman, refers to the fact that at any given time – in science and technology, but also in culture and politics – only certain kinds of next steps are ever feasible. As the science writer Steven Johnson explains, ‘The history of cultural progress is, almost without exception, a story of one door leading to another door, exploring one room at a time.’ The same could apply to a game of chess: at any point in the game, several ingenious moves may be possible, but countless others won’t be. Inventions are no different: the printing press was only possible – and perhaps only thinkable – once moveable type, paper and ink all existed. YouTube, when it was launched in 2005, was a brilliant success. Had it been created in 1995, before broadband and cheap video cameras were widespread, it would have been a terrible idea.

This concept of the adjacent possibly helps to explain the otherwise strange phenomenon of ‘multiples’ – the way certain inventions or discoveries occur in several places, apparently by chance. The wheel seems to have been invented twice: once in the Old World, in an area roughly between the Middle East and Europe, and again, but entirely independently, some 4,000 years later in the New World, in Central America. Electrical batteries were also invented twice, separately, one year apart. People have tried to explain this by vague notions like the fact that certain ideas are just ‘in the air’. But there is a simpler explanation, which is that the innovation in question had simply become part of the adjacent possible. Take the isolation of oxygen as a component of air. It couldn’t have happened before the invention of ultra-sensitive weighing scales. But it also couldn’t have happened before the birth of the idea that air is ‘something’, rather than ‘nothing’, and that it might be made up of gases.

In practical terms, the best way to have new ideas isn’t to take yourself off to a stunning but isolated mountain spot in order to be creative. Rather, you are more likely to succeed if you expand the range of your possible next moves – even if you must attempt to break out of the confines of your circumstances – by exposing yourself to chance, to as many conversations and disagreements and to as many rival and even unrelated ideas as possible, which you can then borrow or put together in some way. This is one way of explaining the amazing new and sometimes revolutionary ideas generated when people get together, whether it’s in Europe’s 17th-century coffee houses, or on the Internet in the 21st century. Good ideas happen when people interact. Contrary to popular opinion, the lone inventor acting in isolation is seldom found in reality.

content: If you want to have new ideas, you might decide to go to an attractive {{36}} , but, in fact, this would be unlikely to achieve the desired results. What you want to do is think outside the {{37}} which might discourage the birth of new ideas. For example, by listening to opposing {{38}} , you can pick and choose among those ideas you find creative. Perhaps by using several ideas in {{39}} you may come up with an invention of your own. It follows that complex {{40}} of relationships are the most favourable environments for innovation.
